rows: This conditional sentence is used to explain that present circumstances would be different if something different had happened in the past.
This conditional sentence is used to express situations in which the outcome is likely (but not guaranteed) to happen in the future.
This conditional sentence expresses general truths or situations in which one thing always causes another.
This conditional sentence is useful for expressing outcomes that are completely unrealistic or will not likely happen in the future.

First Conditional B This conditional sentence is used to express situations in which the outcome is likely (but not guaranteed) to happen in the future. 3. 341b132eeafedb1a6d4f.text: Using Conditionals (Zero, First, Second and Third

62f22e54ac0fc37eb280.text: Conditionals) in Expressing Arguments In your previous lessons, you have learned about conditionals and its type and usage. As a review, a Conditional sentence is a type of sentence that expresses a condition and the outcome or the result of that condition. A condition is something that can occur IF something else happens.

31a0733fc53319107161.text: A Conditional sentence is of a dependent clause and an independent clause that are put together to express the condition and the result.

a07d359e4819e53afbe2.text: Dependent Clause = IF-clause Independent Clause = Main-clause Example:

0003e229138ef67db58e.text: If you stay at home, you will be safer from the threat of the pandemic. The if-clause tells you the condition (If you stay at home) and the main clause tells you the result (you will be safer from the threat of the pandemic).

c3f70a18724f7fa37c7b.text:
We use the zero conditional to talk about things about general truth,
especially for laws and rules.
2. First Conditional

6c93266caa2d1e0b1a4d.text:
We use the first conditional when we talk about the future situation that is
possible to happen or can happen in reality.
3. Second Conditional

92f7d9e0da8c04fad890.text:
The second conditional is used to express the present or future situation
that is impossible or unlikely to happen in reality.
4. Third Conditional

07e0bcb4d2d48b0c9e91.text: The third conditional is used to refer to a time that is in the pastor unreal past condition and express its probable past result.

32753effd2cf2f65640e.text: Conditional sentences are also used to express arguments. Arguments are statements expressing a reason or set of reasons given to persuade others that a certain action or given idea is right or wrong. It is also used to deliver or to present a reason or reasons why you support or oppose an idea or suggestion.

3588f0419506ff1a8fce.text: In expressing arguments using conditional sentences, you are going to present your response as the result from a given condition (if-clause) and/or you will tell the possible or the probable cause of a certain situation or result (main-clause).

6e756bc768de9ce88cd4.text: TYPE OF  VERB FORM   USAGE   CONDITIONAL  IF-CLAUSE MAIN-CLAUSE     0 real condition + present simple present simple  real result       1 possible condition + present simple will + base verb  possible result       2 hypothetical condition + past simple would + base verb  probable result        unreal past condition +  would have + past 3 probable result in the past perfect     participle  past

44031b8eb5bcf7b802f6.text: Example: Situation: Mary’s teacher sent a reminder in their class’ group chat that the

4bdd520e84500f4d04ae.text: submission of their module would be on the day after next. John, one of her classmates, asked her to send him her answer because he forgot to work on his module. If you were Mary, would you help John finish his module by sending him your answers? Why or why not?

8dc43c6c6c7da4d81fda.text: Possible Answer: If I were Mary, I would help John finish his module, but I would not

db2c5bccb2d800a93283.text: send him my answers. I would tell him to start doing his module now and help him out in understanding the lesson. I would also motivate him to answer his module ahead of time so he would not cram the night before the submission.

595c9ce890a613e6cb51.text: Make sure to use the correct type of conditional based on the form/tense of the verb given on the question/situation.

fdb0009aaa3454312856.text: A. Directions: Read the text below entitled “Thank you Ma’am” by Langston Hughes

451c9bf283ba20abda36.text: and reflect on the questions that you will encounter as you read.

e39efc1b1407a39e7bc4.text: She was a large woman with a large purse that had everything in it but hammer and nails. It had a long strap, and she carried it slung across her shoulder. It was about eleven o’clock at night, and she was walking alone, when a boy ran up behind her and tried to snatch her purse. The strap broke with the single tug the boy gave it from behind. But the boy’s weight and the weight of the purse combined caused him to lose his balance so, instead of taking off full blast as he had hoped, the boy fell on his back on the sidewalk, and his legs flew up. The large woman simply turned around and kicked him right square in his blue-jeaned sitter. Then she reached down, picked the boy up by his shirt front, and shook him until his teeth rattled.

df8efc916dab42222c9d.text: After that the woman said, “Pick up my pocketbook, boy, and give it here.” She still held him. But she bent down enough to permit him to stoop and pick up her purse.

a54e59cf764b786379a8.text: Then she said, “Now ain’t you ashamed of yourself?” Firmly gripped by his shirt front, the boy said, “Yes’m.” The woman said, “What did you want to do it for?” The boy said, “I didn’t aim to.” She said, “You a lie!” By that time two or three people passed, stopped, turned to look, and some stood watching.

cf163ffa77eed938e74d.text: “If I turn you loose, will you run?” asked the woman. “Yes’m,” said the boy. “Then I won’t turn you loose,” said the woman. She did not release him. “I’m very sorry, lady, I’m sorry,” whispered the boy.

39ef504f3cd7b5f8d253.text: “Um-hum! And your face is dirty. I got a great mind to wash your face for you. Ain’t you got nobody home to tell you to wash your face?” “No’m,” said the boy. “Then it will get washed this evening,” said the large woman starting up the street, dragging the frightened boy behind her.

3875c1dff6ea4632f013.text: He looked as if he were fourteen or fifteen, frail and willow-wild, in tennis shoes and blue jeans. The woman said, “You ought to be my son. I would teach you right from wrong. Least I can do right now is to wash your face. Are you hungry?”

3f82f58680efe1fc29f8.text: If you were Roger, would you trust Mrs. Jones right away?

202e1a30360581e09845.text: “No’m,” said the being dragged boy. “I just want you to turn me loose.” “Was I bothering you when I turned that corner?” asked the woman.

7ba60ddbb5bd5d9f25fc.text: “No’m.” “But you put yourself in contact with me,” said the woman. “If you think that that contact is not going to last awhile, you got another thought coming. When I get through with you, sir, you are going to remember Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones.”

c6fd1c3a85216bcfd9ab.text: Sweat popped out on the boy’s face and he began to struggle. Mrs. Jones stopped, jerked him around in front of her, put a half-nelson about his neck, and continued to drag him up the street. When she got to her door, she dragged the boy inside, down a hall, and into a large kitchenette- furnished room at the rear of the house. She switched on the light and left the door open. The boy could hear other roomers laughing and talking in the large house. Some of their doors were open, too, so he knew he and the woman were not alone. The woman still had him by the neck in the middle of her room.

be941188251d9e60f073.text: She said, “What is your name?” “Roger,” answered the boy. “Then, Roger, you go to that sink and wash your face,” said the woman, whereupon she turned him loose—at last. Roger looked at the door—looked at the woman—looked at the door—and went to the sink.

f05a00c208cb4407dfc0.text: Let the water run until it gets warm,” she said. “Here’s a clean towel.” “You gonna take me to jail?” asked the boy, bending over the sink.

eb32dd0f4cca4c0b1ab2.text: “Not with that face, I would not take you nowhere,” said the woman. “Here I am trying to get home to cook me a bite to eat, and you snatch my pocketbook! Maybe, you ain’t been to your supper either, late as it be. Have you?”

deab2a94ebaa699bb47a.text: “There’s nobody home at my house,” said the boy. “Then we’ll eat,” said the woman, “I believe you’re hungry—or been hungry— to try to snatch my pocketbook.”

4acd7359527097ce49f8.text: “I wanted a pair of blue suede shoes,” said the boy. “Well, you didn’t have to snatch my pocketbook to get some suede shoes,” said Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones. “You could of asked me.”

6fe41586fa926b084bc6.text: “M’am?” The water dripping from his face, the boy looked at her. There was a long pause. A very long pause. After he had dried his face and not knowing what else to do dried it again, the boy turned around, wondering what next. The door was open. He could make a dash for it down the hall. He could run, run, run, run, run!

477e06723b4134c0e00f.text: If you were Roger, would you run?

8e871eeabf15d81f34b0.text: The woman was sitting on the daybed. After a while she said, “I were young once and I wanted things I could not get.”

679f7db23b097b3d1d30.text: There was another long pause. The boy’s mouth opened. Then he frowned, but not knowing he frowned.

2c845c2bec74b4c25afc.text: The woman said, “Um-hum! You thought I was going to say but, didn’t you? You thought I was going to say, but I didn’t snatch people’s pocketbooks. Well, I wasn’t going to say that.” Pause. Silence. “I have done things, too, which I would not tell you, son—neither tell God, if he didn’t already know. So, you set down while I fix us something to eat. You might run that comb through your hair so you will look presentable.”

b38d74c91279e8389546.text: What did Roger feel at this moment?

bebd00b006d158992f67.text: In another corner of the room behind a screen was a gas plate and an icebox. Mrs. Jones got up and went behind the screen. The woman did not watch the boy to see if he was going to run now, nor did she watch her purse which she left behind her on the daybed. But the boy took care to sit on the far side of the room where he thought she could easily see him out of the corner of her eye, if she wanted to. He did not trust the woman not to trust him. And he did not want to be mistrusted now.

cf626151b96cb13e514a.text: “Do you need somebody to go to the store,” asked the boy, “maybe to get some milk or something?”

8579e7ff3535d3a25907.text: “Don’t believe I do,” said the woman, “unless you just want sweet milk yourself. I was going to make cocoa out of this canned milk I got here.” “That will be fine,” said the boy.

11c04544e8e79aca4be8.text: She heated some lima beans and ham she had in the icebox, made the cocoa, and set the table. The woman did not ask the boy anything about where he lived, or his folks, or anything else that would embarrass him.

7e8dd560ae6dcbfd58c0.text: Instead, as they ate, she told him about her job in a hotel beauty-shop that stayed open late, what the work was like, and how all kinds of women came in and out, blondes, red-heads, and Spanish. Then she cut him a half of her ten-cent cake.

3b3b6fc7ff1cfce185c5.text: “Eat some more, son,” she said. When they were finished eating, she got up and said, “Now, here, take these ten dollars and buy yourself some blue suede shoes. And next time, do not make the mistake of latching onto my pocketbook nor nobody else’s— because shoes come by devilish like that will burn your feet. I got to get my rest now. But I wish you would behave yourself, son, from here on in.”

4782e60eace97d944699.text: Remember the most recent act of kindness you did for someone. Why

3182e2367ed778d10ddf.text: She led him down the hall to the front door and opened it. “Goodnight! Behave yourself, boy!” she said, looking out into the street. The boy wanted to say something else other than “Thank you, m’am” to Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones, but he couldn’t do so as he turned at the barren stoop and looked back at the large woman in the door. He barely managed to say “Thank you” before she shut the door. And he never saw her again. Source: A Journey through Anglo-American Literature, Grade 9 English – Learner’s Manual, First Edition,
